study.title: Acts 21 - Paul's walk to Jerusalem and the beginning of his arrest
study.overview: This chapter shows Paul reaching the decisive point of his trajectory in Acts: he goes to Jerusalem despite the prophetic warnings and, upon arriving, faces false accusations that lead to his arrest. The text highlights the tension between the guidance of the Spirit, the pastoral love of the brethren, Paul's fidelity to the call of Christ and the increasing opposition to the gospel. At the same time, it shows that the mission among the Gentiles did not overturn Paul's bond with his people or his respect for the Jewish community and the temple. The chapter prepares Paul's defense in the following chapters, while revealing that suffering does not interrupt the advancement of God's work.

outline.title: Coastal and farewell trip of the disciples in Tyre
outline.explanation: Paul and his companions follow through various cities of the Eastern Mediterranean to Tyre. There they find disciples, remain seven days and receive from them a warning given by the Spirit that Paul should not go up to Jerusalem. The farewell is marked by public prayer and familial affection, showing a Christian community united by the faith and pain of separation.

outline.title: Arrival to Caesarea and prophetic announcement of suffering
outline.explanation: In Ptolemaida and Caesarea, Paul meets brothers and stays with Philip, one of the seven. Philip's daughters prophesy, and Agabo confirms that Paul will be imprisoned in Jerusalem and handed over to the Gentiles. Despite the thrilled appeals that he will not go, Paul is ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and the church concludes that the will of the Lord should prevail.

outline.title: Reception in Jerusalem and guidance of the elders
outline.explanation: Paul is received willingly by the brethren and relates in detail the work of God among the Gentiles, leading the leaders to glorify the Lord. However, a pastoral and public concern arises: there are rumors that Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses. To avoid scandal and demonstrate that he does not despise the Jewish Law, James and the elders propose that Paul participate in a rite of purification with four men who had vow, while reaffirming the demands already sent to the Gentile believers.

outline.title: riot in the temple and prison of Paul
outline.explanation: When the period of purification is almost completed, Jews from Asia falsely accuse him of teaching against the people, the Law, the temple and of bringing Gentiles to the sacred enclosure. The city agitates, Paul is grabbed, and the Roman commander intervenes to prevent the crowd from killing him. Arrested and conducted under escort, Paul asks permission to speak to the people; the commander, confusing him with an Egyptian rebel, allows speech. Paul then prepares to defend himself, speaking in Hebrew language.

study.context: The chapter takes place during Paul's last approach to Jerusalem, after his long missionary journey between Gentile communities. The text mentions coastal and port places, which combines with the maritime route used by the group. In Jerusalem, the Christian community includes both believing Jews and leaders such as James and the elders, and there is concern for Paul's reputation among zealous Jews of the Law. The climate is of increasing tension: there is faith, hospitality and prayer, but also rumors, misunderstandings and public hostility. The chapter also shows the presence of Roman authority in Jerusalem, which intervenes when the crowd becomes violent.
study.theology: Acts 21 teaches that the will of God can lead the faithful servant to suffering, without this means spiritual defeat. Paul is not shown as a reckless person, but as a resolute person in the face of prophetic warnings and the legitimate affection of the church. The chapter also preserves two truths in tension: salvation in Christ reaches the Gentiles, and at the same time the Christian faith does not need to be read as an automatic contempt for all that is Jewish. Therefore, Paul accepts a public gesture of purification, not as a denial of the gospel, but as an expression of prudence and love for the peace of the church. Moreover, the chapter shows that prophecy is not only prediction; it can serve to prepare the church for suffering. The final response of the community is made to the will of the Lord - summarizes a spirituality of confident submission, even when the path includes arrest and opposition. The false accusation against Paul also reveals how religious zeal can become injustice when separated from the truth. Finally, the commander's intervention shows that God can use civil authorities to curb violence and preserve his servant for the next stage of the mission.

scholarViews.insight: The prophecy of Philip's daughters is presented as a sign of the fulfillment of Joel's promise of the outredding of the Spirit and the exercise of prophetic gifts in the church.
Paul's arrival in Jerusalem marks the transition from his days of missionary service to days of suffering, and the church learns to submit to the will of the Lord when he cannot dissuade him.
Paul spoke to the people of the position of the stairs, out of the direct reach of the crowd and protected by the Roman soldiers, which gave them the conditions to address the people.

questions: How does Paul's response to prophetic warnings help to discern the difference between human prudence and divine calling?
How does the church in Jerusalem try to preserve unity without denying the truth of the gospel between Jews and Gentiles?
What does the chapter teach about how God uses both the suffering and intervention of the authorities to fulfill his purposes?
study.practice: This chapter invites the Christian to obey God even when obedience brings cost, to listen to godly counsel without turning prudence into fear and to seek peace without compromising the truth. In practice, this means accepting correction, avoiding rushed rumors and accusations, maintaining communion with brothers of different convictions at secondary points and trusting that God continues to rule when the path seems to close. It also teaches to value the prayer and loving farewell of the church, especially in times of difficult decision.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain in detail why the disciples by the Spirit told Paul not to go up to Jerusalem; therefore, it is not safe to say whether it was a direct prohibition or prophetic warning interpreted by the disciples. There are also limits to accurately identify the expression translated "Hebrew language" only with the available notes; the understanding that Paul spoke of in the common semiistic language in Judea comes from the notes, but does not allow more specification than this. Moreover, this study depends on the biblical text provided and the excerpts of commentators; it does not add external historical data not mentioned in these sources.
